E64 Local is a cloud-free, LAN-only owner app for the Mahlkönig E64 WS / NG2 grinder.

It has no account, no telemetry, no crash reporting, no analytics and no vendor cloud. The app contacts exactly one host: the device you enter on the setup screen.

Everything it shows comes from the Local Owner API on a development image of your grinder. The action layer is closed by default: it answers 403 until an owner deploys a policy with e64root, and its destructive routes stay blocked until a second flag is deployed as well.

The five action routes are prepare, execute, status, cancel and audit. Prepare validates the route, the parameters, the bounds and the machine state and returns a single-use confirm token.

The token is held in memory only: it is not written to storage, it is not part of any screen state, and it is never logged. Execute sends it back once. When you discard the dialog the token is dropped and nothing runs.

A destructive route cannot be submitted while the device reports destructiveEnabled: false. The app has no override, and the device checks the same flag again before it actuates.

The app talks to the device with two credentials:

1. The vendor session cookie, obtained from the device's own login.
2. An owner token, created by the setup step and written to /db/e64local/token on the device (mode 0600, owner www-data).

The token is 32 random bytes generated on your phone. It is stored encrypted with a key that never leaves the Android Keystore, and it is never logged. There is no recovery path: if it is lost, run the setup again to rotate it.

The device uses a self-signed certificate. Verification is never silently disabled: you are shown the certificate fingerprint and must accept it explicitly before the app stores a pin. Only the pinned certificate is accepted afterwards.
The module only answers when the image is a development build (the first word of /etc/issue is \"development\"). On a production image the module returns 403 and installing it does not change that.

The setup step writes four things: the API module, the root-owned action runner, its token directory and the owner token. It never touches the ESP co-processor, ESP flash or NVS, the bootloader, the eFuse, or any firmware image, and it never uploads firmware. The action layer stays disabled until an owner deploys a policy with e64root; the app can call the five action routes but cannot enable them, and it never reaches the ESP, the bootloader, the eFuse or a firmware image through them.
